brief.situation: You are the information security manager at Ardent Foods, a fictional food producer. At 09:00 your payroll provider sends a vague notice of a 'security incident affecting some customers' API credentials', found three days ago. Your HR system sends it every employee's tax ID and bank details through an API key. Today's payroll file goes to the bank at 10:00. Manage the supplier, protect the payroll and the people in it, and write it up.
handover: The contract's security schedule requires notice within 24 hours of discovery, cooperation with your investigation, logs on request, and the same terms for any subprocessor.
The CFO owns payroll risk; legal counsel decides on notifications to employees and regulators.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. Whoever holds the stolen key works on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you close the incident you notify, record it and explain your reasoning.

source.note: Twenty minutes until the deposit changes is the author's figure.
The bank file cut-off at 10:00 is the fictional company's schedule.
Briefing the risk owner and counsel within the first hour is the author's teaching figure.

readContract.label: Read the notice against the contract's security schedule

effects.finding: Discovery was three days ago; the contract requires notice within 24 hours. The cooperation clause entitles you to their indicators, scope and logs, and binds their subprocessors.

pullLogs.label: Pull the API gateway log for the integration key

effects.finding: Since yesterday 16:20 the key has been used from 203.0.113.45, outside PayCadence's range, reading bank and tax fields.

rotate.label: Rotate the integration key and allow it only from PayCadence's published range

effects.log: The old key stops working; the new one works only from PayCadence's addresses. Payroll is unaffected.
The integration stops: nothing flows either way. The stolen key is still valid, and today's payroll cannot be sent.

resume.label: Resume the integration with the rotated key

The contract is ended and the integration disabled. There is no other payroll provider ready.

writeup.question: For the incident record: how you used the contract, how you contained it without stopping the business, and who you told.

parts.label: The contract
parts.criteria: Reads the notice against the security schedule, records the missed 24-hour clause, invokes cooperation for scope and indicators, and asks about the subprocessor (nth party).
parts.modelAnswer: The supplier was two days past the 24-hour clause; I invoked cooperation, got the indicators and learned the keys were taken from their subprocessor TaxBridge.

parts.label: Containment against the business
parts.criteria: Rotates and restricts the key, which stops the attacker and keeps payroll running; does not suspend or terminate in a way that leaves 1,800 people unpaid; reverts fraudulent deposit changes after out-of-band checks.
parts.modelAnswer: Rotating and restricting the key cut the attacker off without stopping payroll; suspending or terminating would have left everyone unpaid.

parts.label: Communication and treatment
parts.criteria: Escalates to the risk owner and counsel early; leaves employee notification to counsel; records a mitigate treatment with monitoring and an exit plan in the register.
parts.modelAnswer: The CFO and counsel had the facts in the first half hour; counsel decides on employee notice. The register shows a mitigate treatment with subprocessor assurance and an exit plan.

expertPath.text: Read the notice against the contract (two days late); pull your own API log: the key is in use from outside.
Rotate the key and restrict it to the supplier's range; payroll keeps running.
Invoke the cooperation clause (the subprocessor is the source); brief the CFO and counsel; map the data shared.
Register a mitigate treatment with subprocessor assurance and an exit plan; notify the owners; counsel decides on employee notice.

handled.headline: Good: the contract did its job, and so did you
handled.body: A third party's incident is yours to manage through the contract and your own controls. You cut the key off without stopping the business.

handledCostly.headline: Contained, at a cost
handledCostly.body: The criteria show what cost you: changed deposits, a blocked payroll, an unused contract, or a late or out-of-order escalation.

fraud.headline: Pay went to the attacker
fraud.body: Waiting on the supplier left a stolen key valid on payroll day. Your own logs and a key rotation were in your hands from the start.

leftOpen.headline: The stolen key still works
leftOpen.body: The supplier's incident became yours the moment their key reached your data. Rotate and restrict it.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No incident record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Read the notice against the contract: it is two days late, and the cooperation clause entitles you to scope, indicators and logs, including from subprocessors. Check your own logs: the key is being used from outside. Rotate and restrict the key, which stops the attacker and keeps payroll running; suspending or terminating would leave 1,800 people unpaid. Revert any deposit changes after phone checks. Brief the CFO and counsel early and leave employee notification to counsel. Record a mitigate treatment with subprocessor assurance, monitoring and an exit plan.
